name: Peepz Park
blurb: You are an animal in a park with a ball in it. Run into the ball and it rolls; E kicks it properly, and it goes as fast as you were running when you hit it. F is a dash, which is how you catch it. Eat the apples the trees drop. Knock over the critters and the strength bar fills - full, your dash goes rainbow, twice as far, and takes down whatever it touches.

scripts.kick:
/**
 * A ball, and what a kick does to it.
 *
 * The rule beside this one decides *when* - `pressed key: kick, within: 3` - and
 * everything about how hard is here. That split is the point: a rule is a
 * sentence about the game, and how hard you hit a ball is arithmetic.
 *
 * What this script does not do is *move* the ball. The blueprint has a `body`,
 * so gravity, the grass, the trees and the walls all have an opinion about where
 * it goes, and a shoulder into it rolls it with no script at all. Everything
 * below is about the kick, which is the one thing the physics cannot know: how
 * hard, and which way.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * The same kick the pitch has, because this was the old one
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * Reported as *"make the balls like in football, that you kick them not teleport
 * kick them"*, and that is exactly what this was: the park kept the first
 * version of this script while `kickabout` spent four commits fixing it, so the
 * two levels have had different balls for as long as there have been two of
 * them. Three things made the park's read as a teleport rather than a shot, and
 * each is a note of its own below - the power, the loft, and the glow.
 *
 * Momentum, because a ball that always left at the same speed would make running
 * at it pointless. The kicker's pace is measured here rather than asked for, by
 * remembering where they were last frame - a level has no reading of how fast
 * anybody is going, and one frame of positions is exactly that.
 */
const REACH = 3
/**
 * How hard a kick is, and these numbers are the whole of whether it is watchable.
 *
 * They were 9 and 1.7 here, which is a standing kick of nine cells a second and
 * a running one of over thirty. The goals are twenty cells from the middle, so
 * that is a ball which leaves from anywhere, crosses the whole park inside a
 * second and turns up against the far wall - **not a skip in the drawing but a
 * ball that leaves the picture**, which is what "teleport" describes. Traced
 * frame by frame on the pitch next door, the drawn ball was perfectly smooth
 * through the whole of a kick like this and still travelled thirty-one cells.
 *
 * Four and a quarter, the numbers `kickabout` settled on against a pitch this
 * same size. A push leads by about three cells, so a kick is priced at roughly
 * three of those - nine or ten at a walk, a dozen at a sprint - and the ball
 * stays somewhere you can see it the whole way.
 */
const BASE = 4
const CARRY = 0.25
/**
 * Flat. A kick is a force along the ground and gravity does the rest.
 *
 * This lofted at 0.3 of the kick's power to *clear a critter*, which is a real
 * thing to want and not worth what it costs: a hop is the one part of a shot you
 * cannot follow. The ball leaves the ground, its shadow separates from it, and
 * where it comes down is a guess - so every touch read as the ball jumping
 * somewhere rather than being struck. Rolling is legible, and a critter is
 * something to dribble round.
 */
const LOFT = 0

let wasX = null
let wasZ = null
let pace = 0

/**
 * A kick still to be delivered: where it is going, where it started, and how
 * long is left of it.
 *
 * A kick used to be handed to the ball whole, in one frame - the honest sum, and
 * it read as the ball jumping into motion rather than being struck. The same
 * shot spread over a fifth of a second has a visible start to it: the ball
 * accelerates away like something hit hard, which is what it is. Short enough
 * that nothing about aiming or passing changes - the ball is at full speed
 * inside twelve frames.
 *
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * A speed that climbs, and not a stream of little pushes
 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 * The pitch pays this out as impulses - a slice of the kick pushed every frame -
 * and on this grass **that kick does not happen at all**. `REST_SPEED` in the
 * body step stops any grounded body under four tenths of a cell a second, on the
 * argument that a body which creeps is a body somebody reports as drifting; a
 * walking kick sliced across twelve frames is a third of that per frame, so
 * every slice is zeroed in the same frame it arrives and a ball kicked at a walk
 * moves seven centimetres. The pitch escapes it by accident: its ball never
 * quite settles - it micro-bounces a hundredth of a cell forever - so it is not
 * grounded on half its frames and the slices survive. Ours lies still, which is
 * the better-behaved ball and the one the trap catches.
 *
 * So the ramp is on the *speed* rather than on the impulse: the velocity the
 * shot should be doing by now, written whole each frame. Only the first frame or
 * two are under the floor and lost, the ball is at the full number at
 * `SEND_TIME` either way, and it does not depend on the frame rate - which the
 * slices did, doubly: at 144Hz every slice is a third the size and the whole
 * kick disappears on any ball at all.
 *
 * `from` is what it was already doing when it was struck, so a ball rolling
 * towards you still leaves faster than one lying still. Written rather than
 * pushed means `mass` does not divide it, which for a football is the same
 * number - and this is the level's own ball rather than a general verb.
 */
const SEND_TIME = 0.2
const sending = { x: 0, z: 0, fromX: 0, fromZ: 0, left: 0 }

function onTick(dt) {
  const player = getEntityByName('player')

  // How fast they are going, from where they were. Guarded against the first
  // frame and against a teleport, which would otherwise read as a rocket.
  if (player) {
    if (wasX !== null && dt > 0) {
      const moved = Math.sqrt((player.x - wasX) * (player.x - wasX) + (player.z - wasZ) * (player.z - wasZ))
      const speed = moved / dt
      pace = speed > 30 ? pace : speed
    }
    wasX = player.x
    wasZ = player.z
  }

  // The struck ball, brought up to speed over SEND_TIME rather than in a frame.
  if (sending.left > 0 && dt > 0) {
    sending.left = Math.max(0, sending.left - dt)
    const done = 1 - sending.left / SEND_TIME
    self.dx = sending.fromX + sending.x * done
    self.dz = sending.fromZ + sending.z * done
  }

  if (self.get('kicked') > 0) {
    self.set('kicked', 0)
    if (player) {
      const dx = self.x - player.x
      const dz = self.z - player.z
      const away = Math.sqrt(dx * dx + dz * dz)
      if (away < REACH) {
        /**
         * Where you are looking, not where the ball happens to be.
         *
         * This kicked the ball *directly away from the player* - the line from
         * them to it - which makes the shot depend on which side of the ball you
         * happened to arrive at rather than on where you meant it to go. You
         * cannot pass with that: standing a step to the left of the ball sends it
         * right, and the only way to aim was to walk around it.
         *
         * A kick is now the direction you are facing, so it is aimed the same way
         * everything else in the level is aimed - and, the point of the change,
         * **somebody else can read it**. A player who can see which way you are
         * turned can see where the ball is about to go and move to meet it, which
         * is the whole of what makes passing a thing two people do rather than
         * one.
         *
         * `+z` is forward at a facing of zero, which is the frame the spawns, the
         * marks and the race gates all use.
         */
        const facing = (player.rotation * Math.PI) / 180
        const fx = Math.sin(facing)
        const fz = Math.cos(facing)
        const power = BASE + pace * CARRY
        // On top of what it is already doing, so meeting a ball coming towards
        // you sends it on harder than hitting one lying still. Which is the
        // whole of a volley. Ramped rather than struck whole - see SEND_TIME.
        sending.fromX = self.dx
        sending.fromZ = self.dz
        sending.x = fx * power
        sending.z = fz * power
        sending.left = SEND_TIME
        self.emit('kicked')
      }
    }
  }

  /*
   * No material change any more, and it is worth recording why. The ball turned
   * to rainbow glass while it was going somewhere, as a beacon that read across
   * the park. But the swap itself is a discontinuity: the frame you kick, the
   * ball you were looking at becomes a glass one the grass shows straight
   * through, and on the pitch next door every report of the kick "jumping"
   * survived every fix to the physics because the thing jumping was the look.
   * Its own colours are the most visible thing this ball can wear, at any speed,
   * from anywhere.
   */
}

/**
 * It met the level - the grass, a tree, the back of a goal.
 *
 * The event that did not exist while the ball was a script: nothing could tell
 * you it had *arrived* anywhere, because nothing ever did. `other` is null on a
 * hit; a rule about touching a critter is a `collide`.
 */
function onTrigger(event) {
  if (event === 'hit' && self.speed > 6) self.emit('thump')
}
scripts.falling:
/**
 * An apple on its way down, and then lying there.
 *
 * Entities have no gravity - the character controller is the only thing in this
 * engine that falls - so a thing that should drop does it here. Which is fine
 * for one apple and is the honest reason it is a script rather than a field.
 */
const GRAVITY = 14
const GROUND = 1.2

let fall = 0

function onTick(dt) {
  if (self.y <= GROUND) {
    self.y = GROUND
    fall = 0
    // Turning slowly where it lies, so it reads as something to pick up.
    self.rotation = (self.rotation + dt * 45) % 360
    return
  }
  fall += GRAVITY * dt
  self.y = Math.max(GROUND, self.y - fall * dt)
}
